title: Compound nouns and noun phrases
subtitle: an address book / a lion's den / a cup of tea
summary: Decide between noun + noun, noun + -'s + noun and noun + preposition + noun, and use compound nouns made from two-word verbs.

lesson.heading: noun + noun
lesson.text: In a compound made of noun + noun, the second noun usually gives the general class of thing and the first noun says what type it is. The first noun normally has a **singular** form.

examples.text: **a shoe shop**, **a coal mine**, **a computer programmer**, **a film star**

lesson.note: To make the compound plural we usually make the second noun plural: coal mine(s), office-worker(s), tea leaf / leaves.

lesson.heading: When the first noun stays plural
lesson.text: There are exceptions. The first noun is plural when it only *has* a plural form, and when we refer to an institution (an industry, a department, etc.) that deals with more than one kind of item or activity.

examples.text: **a savings account**, **a customs officer**, **a clothes shop**, **the arms trade**
examples.note: arms = weapons; compare a shoe shop
glasses = spectacles. Compare a glass case = a case made of glass
arts = music, drama, film, dance, painting. Compare an art festival; art = painting, drawing and sculpture
different types of building material, different forms of publication

lesson.heading: noun + -'s + noun
lesson.text: We prefer the possessive form when the first noun is the **user** of the item in the second noun, and when the thing in the second noun is **produced by** the thing (often an animal) in the first.

examples.text: **a baby's bedroom**, **a lion's den**, **a women's clinic**, **a girls' school**, **birds' nests**

examples.note: but lamb chops and chicken drumsticks

lesson.heading: Parts of people, parts of things

left.label: Parts of people and animals: noun + -'s + noun

lesson.heading: noun + preposition + noun
lesson.text: We prefer a preposition when we talk about a **container together with its contents**, and when the combination does not refer to a well-known class of items.

examples.note: = a cup with tea in it; compare a tea cup = a cup for drinking tea from

lesson.heading: Compounds from verbs + prepositions
lesson.text: Some compound nouns are made up of verbs and prepositions or adverbs, and are related to a two- or three-word verb. Countable ones make their plural with *-s* at the end, but a few put it in the middle.

examples.text: Mansen **broke out of** the prison by dressing as a woman. = escaped
There was a major **break-out** from the prison last night. = prisoners escaped

lesson.heading: Hyphenated phrases before a noun
rows: the day-to-day running of the company
progressing from one stage to the next

lesson.text: Ask yourself *who or what uses it, and who or what made it*: a user or a producer points to *-'s* (a girls' school, cow's milk), while a part of an object points to plain noun + noun (a pen top).

exercises.prompt: Ali worked in the parks department, but a few years ago he retrained and now he's ___.
exercises.explanation: In noun + noun the first noun normally stays singular: a computer programmer.

exercises.statement: Of course, what he really wants to be is a films star!
exercises.explanation: ... what he really wants to be is a film star. The first noun of the compound stays singular.

exercises.prompt: Someone got out of a car without looking and ___ hit her.
exercises.explanation: For parts of things we use noun + noun, not the possessive: the car door.

exercises.prompt: I was waiting at the bus stop when a cyclist on her way to the ___ up the road got knocked off her bike.
exercises.explanation: The pupils are the users of the school, so we use noun + -'s + noun: a girls' school.

exercises.prompt: Which pattern does each phrase use?
I've just got three things on my shopping list - ___, a packet of biscuits and some toothpaste.
exercises.explanation: A container together with its contents takes noun + preposition + noun, not a milk bottle.

exercises.prompt: Match each two-word verb with the compound noun that comes from it.

exercises.statement: Marta hated going into her grandfather's old tools shed. It was full of spiders' webs.
exercises.explanation: ... her grandfather's old tool shed. It was full of spiders' webs. The first noun of the compound is singular (tool shed), but the webs are produced by the spiders, so spiders' webs is right.

exercises.prompt: When Jake was cleaning his armchair he found his ___ with his sunglasses inside.
exercises.explanation: glasses only has a plural form, so it stays plural: a glasses case. Compare a glass case = a case made of glass.

exercises.prompt: The tracks on his latest CD range from love songs to ___.
exercises.explanation: 'Pollution songs' is not a well-known class of songs, so we use noun + preposition + noun.

exercises.prompt: Match each hyphenated phrase with its meaning.

pairs.right: progressing from one stage to the next

exercises.prompt: The party will never regain power unless it can persuade ___ voters that it has rid itself of corruption.
exercises.explanation: Hyphenated phrases like middle-of-the-road go before the noun to say more precisely what it refers to.
